\chapter{Introduction}\label{introduction}

\section{Background}\label{background}

``Is the game hard enough for the intended player?'' is one of the key
questions that game designers keep asking during development
\autocite{weber2020}. A game that is too hard drives players away while
one that is too easy soon becomes stale, both of which risk losing
players and receiving a negative reception \autocite{karavidas2022}.
That is why difficulty can be an indicator of player engagement and
experience \autocite{romero2023,alvarado2021}. Designers measure this
difficulty through playtesting. However, manual playtesting is
resource-intensive since it needs many testers over many sessions and
has to be repeated after every significant design change
\autocite{weber2020,prasetya2026,zhao2025}. For indie game developers
with limited budgets, this cost is often prohibitive. Thus, they need a
cheaper way to obtain difficulty data that still reflects human players.

Automatic playtesting has gained popularity among industry and academic
researchers alike. The methods explored so far fall into two groups.
Hand-crafted methods, such as programmed test agents
\autocite{prasetya2026} and mathematical difficulty models
\autocite{francillette2025}, require heavy engineering effort for each
game or genre. Learning-based methods such as deep reinforcement
learning need large training resources while also tending to play in
ways that humans would not \autocite{delfosse2025}. Large Language
Models (LLMs) provide an alternative, as LLM agents can play games
ranging from chess \autocite{feng2023} to Pokémon battles
\autocite{hu2024} and Minecraft \autocite{wang2023} using only a text
description of the rules. Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025} show that
the difficulty LLM agents experience in Wordle and Slay the Spire
follows that of human players, even though the agents play worse.
However, these LLM playtesters rely on a single agent that plays with
only one playstyle. Human players are more diverse, as some take risks
while others play safely. The difficulty that matters to a designer is
the one experienced by this diverse population. Moreover, single LLMs
replicate human strategic behavior less closely than multi-agent systems
do \autocite{sreedhar2025}. Thus, it remains unclear whether an LLM
playtester can produce difficulty data that is both consistent and
aligned with human players once multiple playstyles are considered.

To accommodate this gap, we establish a persona-based multi-agent LLM
debate framework that acts as an automated playtester. Such a playtester
plays a game through the same actions available to a human player while
recording the outcome of each playthrough. Game difficulty here refers
to objective difficulty, which is the part of difficulty measured from
play outcomes rather than the difficulty perceived by individual players
\autocite{constant2017}. In this framework, several LLM agents with
different playstyle personas debate each in-game decision until they
reach consensus on the action to play. In other words, the agents reach
consensus on what to play rather than on how hard the game is. The
difficulty data comes from the outcome of each playthrough, such as the
number of guesses used. These outcomes are then compared with human
performance baselines, which are the average results of real players on
the same puzzles. The exact agent roles and debate protocol are defined
later in the research method.

We employ Wordle as the case study for three reasons. First, its games
are short with deterministic feedback. Second, it was studied by Xiao
and Yang \autocite{xiao2025}, so our results can be related to prior
single-agent work. Third, Wordle has public per-puzzle human results
\autocite{engagingdata} that express the difficulty of each puzzle as
the average number of guesses human players needed. The playtester plays
a sample of historical puzzles several times each, after which we
measure how much its outcomes vary across repeated runs of the same
puzzle. We also measure how well its average guess counts agree with the
human averages, both as continuous scores and as ordered difficulty
categories. In addition, we describe how the playstyle personas behave
during the debate, since a persona-based playtester is only meaningful
when its personas actually shape the guesses.

\section{Problem Statement}\label{problem-statement}

The background shows that game designers still lack an automated
playtester whose outcomes can serve as evidence of game difficulty for
human players. Existing LLM playtesters use a single agent with one
playstyle \autocite{xiao2025}, while the difficulty that matters to a
designer is the one experienced by a diverse player population. For a
persona-based playtester to fill this gap, two conditions must hold
before its outcomes can be used as difficulty data. First, the outcomes
must be consistent across runs. Since LLM outputs vary between calls,
the same puzzle can end differently on different runs, which leaves a
designer with little to rely on. Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025} play
each Wordle puzzle 20 times yet report only the average outcome, so this
consistency is still unknown. Second, the outcomes must agree with human
difficulty \autocite{xiao2025}, because a consistent playtester that
finds every puzzle equally easy is still of no use. Moreover, the
playtester is only persona-based in practice if its personas keep their
playstyles during the debate. Debating LLM agents may conform to their
peers instead of keeping their assigned personas \autocite{baltaji2024},
which would leave a single playstyle behind the outcomes. This research
therefore examines whether the proposed playtester meets both conditions
in Wordle while describing how its personas behave.

\section{Research Questions}\label{research-questions}

Based on the problem statement, this research addresses the following
research questions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{RQ1.} How consistent are the Wordle playtest outcomes produced
  by the persona-based multi-agent debate playtester across repeated
  runs on the same puzzles?
\item
  \textbf{RQ2.} To what extent do the Wordle difficulty estimates
  derived from the playtester's outcomes agree with human difficulty,
  measured by average guess scores and difficulty categories?
\item
  \textbf{RQ3.} How do the playstyle personas behave during the debate,
  and how strongly do their suggestions shape the final guesses?
\end{itemize}

Answering RQ1 and RQ2 shows whether the playtester can be trusted as a
source of difficulty data for Wordle, which is the first step toward
solving the general problem. RQ3 shows whether the personas actually
take part in producing that data.

\section{Research Objectives}\label{research-objectives}

The objectives of this research are fourfold:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  To implement a persona-based multi-agent LLM debate playtester for
  Wordle, in which agents with different playstyle personas reach
  consensus on each guess while every playthrough is logged as
  difficulty data.
\item
  To measure the consistency of the playtester's outcomes across
  repeated runs of the same puzzles, which answers RQ1.
\item
  To measure the agreement between the playtester's difficulty estimates
  and human performance baselines using both average guess scores and
  difficulty categories, which answers RQ2.
\item
  To describe how each playstyle persona behaves during the debate and
  how often its suggestions are adopted in the final guesses, which
  answers RQ3.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Scope and Limitations}\label{scope-and-limitations}

This research focuses on Wordle as a single case study. The playtester
plays past Wordle puzzles for which public human results are available
\autocite{engagingdata}, so that every outcome has a human counterpart
to compare with. Game difficulty is limited to objective difficulty,
which is measured from how many guesses the playtester needs to solve
each puzzle \autocite{constant2017}. The playtester is evaluated as a
whole system, judged by how consistent its outcomes are and how closely
they agree with human players. The behavior of the personas is described
from the debate records rather than tested by removing or swapping
personas.

This research also has several limitations. It does not compare the
debate playtester with a single-agent playtester
\autocite{sreedhar2025}. Its persona analysis is also descriptive, so it
shows how the personas take part in the debate without proving that any
persona causes the outcomes. Moreover, the human baselines describe
players as a group rather than as individuals, so the comparison can
only be made for each puzzle as a whole. The difficulty perceived by
players is not studied either \autocite{constant2017}, since no human
participants are involved. Finally, the findings apply to Wordle and to
the LLM used in this research, while other games such as Slay the Spire
\autocite{xiao2025} may behave differently.

\section{Expected Contributions}\label{expected-contributions}

This research is expected to contribute in four ways. First, it offers
an automated playtester in which LLM agents with different playstyles
decide together how to play a game. Second, it shows whether such a
playtester gives similar results when it plays the same game again.
Third, it shows how closely the difficulty found by the playtester
follows the difficulty experienced by human players. Fourth, it shows
how the playstyle personas take part in the debate, which reveals
whether they actually shape the play.

For indie game developers, these results indicate whether an LLM
playtester can provide difficulty data that reflects human players,
which would reduce their reliance on manual playtesting
\autocite{prasetya2026,zhao2025}. For researchers, this research extends
earlier work on LLM playtesters \autocite{xiao2025} from a single agent
to several agents with different playstyles \autocite{sreedhar2025}.

\chapter{Literature Review}\label{literature-review}

\section{Automated Game Playtesting}\label{automated-game-playtesting}

Playtesting lets players try a game under development so that designers
can see how the game is actually experienced. It reveals faults in the
game as well as problems in its design, such as levels that turn out
harder than intended \autocite{weber2020}. However, manual playtesting
depends on many human testers over many sessions, which makes it
resource-intensive to repeat after every design change
\autocite{prasetya2026,zhao2025}. Automated playtesting reduces this
cost by letting software agents play the game while recording what
happens.

The earliest automated playtesters are hand-crafted. Prasetya et al.
\autocite{prasetya2026} use the APLib framework to build highly
controlled test agents through goal structures and domain-specific
languages. However, building such agents requires significant
programming effort with a steep learning curve. Francillette et al.
\autocite{francillette2025} propose a mathematical model that evaluates
the difficulty of platformer games automatically. Their model is
deterministic and needs no sophisticated AI, yet it is limited to the
platformer genre while demanding a complex setup.

Learning-based playtesters remove part of this manual work. Gudmundsson
et al. \autocite{gudmundsson2018} train a deep neural network on human
moves in a puzzle game, after which it plays new levels to predict their
difficulty for players. Such an agent needs a large set of human play
data before it can be used. Deep reinforcement learning agents learn
from their own play instead, yet they need large training resources.
Even when these agents outperform human players, they lack the natural
behavioral patterns of human play \autocite{delfosse2025}. Holmgård et
al. \autocite{holmgard2019} narrow this gap through procedural personas,
which are agents tuned to represent different playstyles. Their personas
show that a playtester can cover more than one way of playing, although
each persona still relies on heuristics evolved for the specific game.

LLM-based playtesters are the most recent group. LLM agents receive the
rules and the current game state as text, so they can play a new game
without game-specific training \autocite{xiao2025}. Zhao and Tang
\autocite{zhao2025} focus on match-3 games, where they address the
inability of an LLM to ``see'' the game by converting the board into
numerical representations. Their playtester reaches strong code coverage
while detecting bugs effectively. Bateni and Whitehead
\autocite{bateni2024} show that LLM agents in Slay the Spire can plan
over a long horizon without specialized training, which lets them adapt
to changes in the game rules. Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025} go
further by using LLM agents to measure the difficulty of Wordle and Slay
the Spire. Their agents play worse than humans, yet the difficulty
patterns the agents experience resemble those of human players. However,
a single LLM loses too often in most games, so the authors need a
handicap system to prevent this. These studies make LLMs a promising
option for indie game developers, who rarely have the data or budget
that learning-based methods need.

\section{Game Difficulty and Behavioral Performance
Measures}\label{game-difficulty-and-behavioral-performance-measures}

Difficulty is closely linked to whether a game is fun. Players may feel
a sense of accomplishment when they overcome challenges, particularly
when those challenges are significant \autocite{karavidas2022}. For
example, Dark Souls was regarded as one of the hardest games of its
time, yet the higher the risk a player takes, the greater the reward
\autocite{guzsvinecz2024}. Its difficulty drew strong player engagement,
which later gave rise to a new sub-genre known as ``souls-like''
\autocite{klepek2017}. That is why measuring difficulty for the intended
player is an important part of game design.

According to Constant et al. \autocite{constant2017}, difficulty can be
viewed from two sides. Subjective difficulty is how challenging players
perceive the game to be, which is hard to measure directly because it is
tied to personal skill, stress and emotion. Objective difficulty is the
measurable part of difficulty that comes from how players actually
perform, independent of their perception. This research is concerned
with objective difficulty only, because an automated playtester produces
play outcomes rather than perceptions of the game.

Objective difficulty is measured through behavioral performance
measures, which are records of what players do and achieve while
playing. Typical measures include whether a challenge is completed, how
many attempts it takes and how long it takes. Dynamic difficulty
adjustment systems use the same kind of measures to judge the skill of a
player during play \autocite{weber2020,romero2023}. Playtesting studies
use them to compare agents with humans, such as the level success rate
of an agent against the pass rate of human players
\autocite{gudmundsson2018}.

In Wordle, the natural performance measure is the number of guesses a
player needs to find the answer. Fewer guesses indicate an easier
puzzle, while more guesses or a lost game indicate a harder one.
Engaging Data \autocite{engagingdata} publishes the guess distribution
of real players for each past puzzle, from which the average number of
guesses per puzzle can be computed. For example, a puzzle that players
solve in 3.2 guesses on average is objectively easier than one that
takes 5.8 guesses. However, the dataset does not provide further details
such as the demographics of the players. This average serves as the
human performance baseline in this research, as it does in the Wordle
comparison of Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025}.

Comparing a playtester with humans raises two separate questions. The
first is whether the playtester gives similar outcomes when it plays the
same puzzle again, since a single run of an LLM agent may not represent
its typical play. The variation of outcomes across repeated runs, such
as their standard deviation, shows how reliable the playtester is. The
second question is whether its outcomes rank and group puzzles the same
way human results do. Agreement can be checked on continuous scores,
such as the correlation between average guess counts, or on ordered
categories that range from easy to hard. Since the human baselines
describe the player population rather than individual players, these
comparisons are made per puzzle over a random sample of puzzles.

\section{Related Work}\label{related-work}

LLM agents have been shown to play a wide range of games. ChessGPT
combines policy learning with language modeling for chess
\autocite{feng2023}, while PokeLLMon reaches human-parity performance in
Pokémon battles \autocite{hu2024}. Voyager acts as an embodied agent in
Minecraft that keeps learning new skills as it explores
\autocite{wang2023}. These agents aim to play well rather than to play
like humans, which is a different goal from playtesting.

For playtesting, the key question is whether the results of an agent
reflect human players. The LLM playtesters reviewed above play alone
with a single playstyle \autocite{zhao2025,xiao2025}, so the variety of
human play is not represented. Sreedhar and Chilton
\autocite{sreedhar2025} show in a strategic game that multi-agent
systems replicate human behavior more closely than single LLMs do.
Before LLMs, Holmgård et al. \autocite{holmgard2019} already represented
different players through personas with different playstyles. More
recently, MIMIC \autocite{chen2025} gives an LLM game tester different
personality traits, which leads to more diverse solutions with higher
test coverage. Thus, a playtester that captures this variety needs to
move beyond a single LLM agent.

Multi-agent debate is one way to combine several LLM agents into one
decision. In a debate, agents propose answers before reading the
reasoning of the others, after which they revise their answers over
several rounds until they agree \autocite{du2024}. Du et al.
\autocite{du2024} show that this process improves factual accuracy and
reasoning compared with a single agent. Liang et al.
\autocite{liang2024} let agents express arguments in a state of ``tit
for tat'', where each agent responds directly to the position of the
previous one. A managing agent oversees this exchange to reach the final
decision. ChatEval \autocite{chan2024} gives agents different roles in a
debate for evaluating text, while finding that the diversity of these
roles is important for its results. However, Smit et al.
\autocite{smit2024} find that debate does not reliably outperform other
prompting strategies, as its results depend strongly on how the debate
is set up. Personas also do not always hold in a debate, since agents
may conform to their peers or drift away from their assigned views
\autocite{baltaji2024}.

This research follows the debate structure of Liang et al.
\autocite{liang2024} for two reasons. First, its managing agent gives a
single point where the arguments end in one action, which a playtester
needs because every turn must produce a playable move. Second, agents
that argue from different positions keep the debate from collapsing into
immediate agreement, which matches the role of playstyle personas
\autocite{chan2024}. Since its benefit depends on the setup
\autocite{smit2024}, this research evaluates the resulting playtester
directly rather than assuming that debate improves it.

\section{Research Gap and
Positioning}\label{research-gap-and-positioning}

The reviewed work shows a trade-off between generality and human
likeness. Hand-crafted playtesters are precise but must be rebuilt for
each game \autocite{prasetya2026,francillette2025}. Learning-based
playtesters need either large sets of human play data or large training
resources \autocite{gudmundsson2018,delfosse2025}. LLM playtesters can
play a new game from its rules alone, while the difficulty they
experience can follow that of human players \autocite{xiao2025}.
However, existing LLM playtesters use a single agent with one playstyle,
even though personas have long been used to represent different players
\autocite{holmgard2019}.

Multi-agent debate could reconcile these different playstyles into one
consensus action, yet automated consensus frameworks remain absent from
current difficulty measurement methods. Three questions therefore remain
open. First, LLM outputs vary between calls, so it is unclear whether a
playtester built from several debating agents gives consistent outcomes
across repeated runs. Even Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025} play each
Wordle puzzle 20 times yet report only the average outcome. Second, it
is unclear whether the difficulty found by such a playtester still
agrees with human performance baselines. Third, it is unclear whether
the personas keep their playstyles during the debate, since debating
agents may conform to their peers \autocite{baltaji2024}. To the best of
our knowledge, no prior study has applied persona-based multi-agent
debate to measure game difficulty.

This research is positioned where these lines of work meet. It takes
playstyle personas from persona-based playtesting
\autocite{holmgard2019} while taking the consensus process from
multi-agent debate \autocite{liang2024}. Both are then applied to the
LLM difficulty measurement of Xiao and Yang \autocite{xiao2025}, using
Wordle and its public human results \autocite{engagingdata}. Unlike
studies that compare multi-agent systems with a single agent
\autocite{sreedhar2025,smit2024}, this research validates the playtester
as a system. It does so through the consistency of its outcomes (RQ1),
their agreement with human difficulty (RQ2) and the behavior of its
personas during the debate (RQ3).
